notes.meaning: Paul calls the believers to find their joy in the Lord, not in outward things. That kind of joy is a strong guard against false teaching. He does not mind repeating what he taught them before, because hearing important truths again helps us remember them and keeps us safe.

Paul says "watch out" three times. He is warning against teachers who said Christians must keep the Jewish law and be circumcised (cut as a sign of belonging to God's people) in order to be saved. Some Jews called outsiders "dogs," and Paul turns that name back on these teachers. He calls their circumcision a mere "cutting" of the body, because they trusted in it instead of in Christ, and they cut up the church.

Those who trust in Christ are the true people of God. Their circumcision is a change of heart, not a mark on the body. They worship by the help of God's Spirit, they boast in Jesus, and they do not rely on "the flesh." That means any outward thing, such as birth, rituals or human effort.

Paul is not putting these things down because he lacked them. If anyone could boast in outward privileges, he could, even more than his opponents. That shows he gave them up because he saw their true worth, not out of envy.

Paul lists his record. He was circumcised on the eighth day just as the law said, born a true Israelite from the tribe of Benjamin, and a Hebrew through both parents. He was a Pharisee, part of the strictest group in keeping God's law. His zeal was so great that he hunted down Christians. As far as people could see, he kept the law without fault, though that was outward keeping, not perfect holiness before God.

All the things Paul once counted as profit, he now writes on the loss side of the ledger because of Christ. They were worse than useless, because his pride in them kept him from coming to Christ. We come to Christ empty-handed, not trusting our own goodness.

Paul goes further: he counts everything as loss next to the great worth of knowing Jesus as his Lord. He really did lose much to follow Christ. Yet he calls it all "rubbish," a strong word for refuse or dung thrown to dogs. The things were not evil in themselves. Trusting them in place of Christ was the problem.

Paul wants to be found joined to Christ, especially on the day he stands before God. He does not want to rely on his own "righteousness," meaning his own goodness from keeping the law. He wants the righteousness that comes from God and is received through faith in Christ. Faith is the hand that receives the gift, not the thing that earns it.

differ.view: This righteousness is Christ's own goodness credited to the believer, like clothing put on him, apart from any works.
This is also an inward righteousness worked in us by God's Spirit through faith. It is not only about being declared right with God, but about being made holy.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some translations read "through the faithfulness of Christ" instead of "through faith in Christ." They note the grammar can go either way, and that this reading does not deny faith in Christ.

notes.meaning: Paul longs to know Christ personally, not just facts about Him. He wants to feel the power of Christ's resurrection raising him to new life. He also wants to share in Christ's sufferings by bearing hardship for Him. Being "conformed to His death" means dying to sin and to the world, as Christ died for sin.

Paul's goal is the glorious resurrection of believers on the last day. The word "somehow" does not mean he doubted. It shows how hard and earnest the struggle is, and his humble hope. He hoped to reach it through Christ's merit, not his own, and a holy fear of falling short kept him pressing on.

differ.view: Some believe Paul was probably thinking of the Rapture, when Christ takes His people to Himself, and hoped to live to see it.

notes.meaning: Paul admits he has not yet reached the goal or been made perfect. So he keeps running hard, like a racer chasing the prize. He wants to grab hold of the thing for which Christ first grabbed hold of him. Christ taking hold of us comes first, and that is our safety.

differ.view: Paul plainly says he was not free from sin. Even the most devoted believer never reaches perfection while on earth.
Paul is not confessing remaining sin. "Not yet perfected" means he had not yet finished his race and received the prize. Believers can still pursue perfect holiness, or love for God, in this life.
Paul denies being perfected here but counts himself among the "perfect" in verse 15. He was perfect, but not yet perfected.
Paul was complete as a new person in Christ and in being made right with God, but not yet in how far he had grown.

notes.meaning: Paul repeats that he has not arrived. His one aim is to forget what lies behind and stretch toward what lies ahead, like a runner leaning toward the finish. Forgetting does not mean erasing the past. It means not resting on past success or being stuck in past failure.

Paul keeps running toward the finish line to win the prize. That prize is the life of heaven to which God calls every Christian. The calling comes from heaven and leads to heaven. It comes only in Christ Jesus, not by our own strength.

Paul asks all "mature" believers, those grown up in faith, to share this attitude: trust Christ alone and keep pressing on. If some see things differently, God will make it clear to them in time. Meanwhile Christians should bear with one another on smaller matters.
Even while waiting for more light, we must keep living by what we already understand. We should not lose the ground we have gained. God gives more to those who walk in what they already know.

Paul invites the church to copy his example together, as he copies Christ. They should also look closely at others who live the same way, like Timothy and Epaphroditus. Not everyone is a good model to follow.

With tears, Paul warns about many who claim Christ but live as enemies of His cross. Their stomach, or appetites, is their god. They boast in what should shame them, and their minds are fixed on earthly things. Their road ends in destruction. Older writers differ on who they were: false teachers pushing the law, or people who used freedom as an excuse for loose living.

Christians are citizens of heaven. Philippi was a Roman colony whose people were proud to be Roman citizens. In the same way, believers belong to heaven while living here as strangers. So we eagerly wait for our Savior, the Lord Jesus, to come back from there.

When Jesus returns, He will change our weak bodies, which suffer sickness and death, to be like His own glorious body. It will be the same body, but changed in form. He can do this by the same mighty power that lets Him rule over all things, even death.
